stories.title: Hogan Lovells Cadwalader, the Blockbuster New Firm in Corporate Law
stories.excerpt: You know that nightmare, where you are late for class and your teacher calls out from behind you, and all you feel is dread? That happened to real estate lawyer Sulie Arias, a partner with the corporate finance practice at Hogan Lovells Cadwalader — a newly formed firm thanks to a $3.9 billion merger — except her reality wasn’t a nightmare. The professor was running to catch up with Arias to tell the trembling student just how impressed she was with the grade Arias received on a test that very few people had even passed. The professor encouraged Arias to pursue law as a career, and now she is part of one of the biggest law firms in the country, working alongside people like Trevor Adler, another partner in the corporate finance practice. Hogan Lovells Cadwalader is the result of the almost $4 billion merger between Hogan Lovells, and Cadwalader Wickersham & Taft that took effect on July 1, creating a singular firm. Commercial Observer caught up with Arias and Adler in August to discuss the merger, their careers and practices, insights on office leasing and the other real estate markets in New York City, as well as the benefits of the merger. This conversation has been edited for length and clarity. Commercial Observer: Please introduce yourselves and tell us about your practice. Trevor Adler: I am from the legacy Hogan Lovell side. I am a lifer with my particular group of people. I started as a summer associate in 2006, and have been with the same real estate team ever since. There are a lot of lifers in our combined team too. I do all things real estate, but my specialty is condominiums and commercial leasing — office, retail, medical, data centers — on both the landlord and tenant side, about half my work is in the New York City area, and about half is across the country. Also, I just love history and I have written a LinkedIn post every week since January about New York City real estate history. Sulie Arias: I’ve been with Cadwalader for six years, and before
bullets: Hogan Lovells + Cadwalader merger creates $3.9B legal powerhouse
Real estate finance practice now expanded with combined expertise
No direct multifamily supply, demand, capital, or cost signal
stories.summary: Hogan Lovells and Cadwalader Wickersham & Taft merged July 1, 2024, forming a combined $3.9 billion firm. The combined entity consolidates corporate finance and real estate practices. This is a structural legal market event with no material impact on multifamily development fundamentals.
stories.impact: Minimal relevance. While law firm consolidation can affect CRE transaction velocity and fee structures, this story contains no specific intelligence on development financing, market growth, or cost drivers affecting multifamily underwriting in any market.

stories.title: Investment Firm Capital Group Takes 70K SF at Rudin’s 345 Park Avenue
stories.excerpt: Global investment management firm Capital Group is taking space for an additional office in New York City. Capital Group, which is based in Los Angeles and oversees $3.6 trillion in assets, signed a 10-year lease for the entire 70,400-square-foot fourth floor of Rudin’s 345 Park Avenue in Midtown, according to the landlord. The firm will open its new office in the fall of 2027. “345 Park Avenue’s prime location, large floor plates and our upcoming amenity enhancements distinguish it as a best-in-class asset,” Michael Rudin, co-CEO at Rudin, said in a statement. “We are pleased to accommodate Capital Group’s continued growth in the Plaza District and commitment to New York City.” The lease is part of a $38 million investment by Capital Group that is expected to create 200 new jobs in the city over the next five years, according to Crain’s New York Business, which first reported news of the lease. Gov. Kathy Hochul is expected to announce the news Tuesday and the state’s backing of the investment. “Capital Group is making its largest investment ever in its sales force to create two new client coastal hubs in Los Angeles and New York and expand our presence in both,” Matt Eisenhardt, head of sales for the advisor group at Capital Group, wrote in a LinkedIn post in April. Eisenhardt added that as part of the expansion, the firm plans to hire 130 new sales and sales support roles to reach more advisors. The new deal at 345 Park Avenue represents a second New York City office for Capital Group, which will continue to operate its city headquarters out of a roughly 25,000-square-foot space three blocks north at BXP’s 399 Park Avenue. The asking rent was unclear, but a report from Newmark found office rents along Park Avenue in Midtown averaged $127.78 per square foot during the second quarter of 2026. bullets: Capital Group leases 70.4K SF at 345 Park Ave, Manhattan; 10-year term

stories.summary: Capital Group (LA-based, $3.6T AUM) signed a 10-year lease for the entire 4th floor (70,400 SF) at Rudin's 345 Park Avenue in Midtown Manhattan, with occupancy Fall 2027. The firm will invest $38M and create 200 jobs over five years. This lease demonstrates continued Manhattan office strength and confidence from major institutional tenants.
stories.impact: Signals sustained office-sector resilience in Manhattan's Plaza District, which has ripple effects for mixed-use development and ground-floor retail demand in Midtown submarkets. Large employer expansions drive white-collar worker in-migration, strengthening nearby residential rental demand; however, multifamily developers should monitor whether office flight to suburban submarkets (NJ, CT, Westchester) redistributes demand away from Manhattan core.

stories.title: CBRE Scores Charleston-Area Warehouse Leasing Assignment
stories.excerpt: CBRE has been retained to market and lease North Rhett Center at 5801 North Rhett Avenue, a 516,000-square-foot two-building industrial property in Hanahan, South Carolina. The property offers approximately 318,926 square feet of available space for lease and was recently acquired by Obelisk Real Estate Partners. CBRE’s Brendan Redeyoff and Bob Barrineau are leading leasing efforts on behalf of Obelisk Real Estate Partners. Obelisk Real Estate Partners recently acquired 5801 North Rhett Avenue and the adjacent 305,250-square foot industrial property at 1020 North Pointe Industrial Boulevard from CenterPoint Properties. The available space at 5801 North Rhett can accommodate users ranging from approximately 50,000 square feet to the full 318,926 square feet. The property also offers CSX rail service and up to 3.25 acres of laydown yard space, providing flexibility for a range of manufacturing, logistics and distribution users. The asset is also proximate to the NIWC and Charleston International Airport, where Boeing is expanding its production facility. bullets: Obelisk RE acquired 823K SF industrial portfolio in Hanahan, SC

stories.summary: Obelisk Real Estate Partners acquired a 516K SF two-building industrial property (North Rhett Center) plus adjacent 305K SF asset in Hanahan, South Carolina, from CenterPoint Properties. CBRE is marketing 318,926 SF of available space, with flexibility for users 50K–319K SF. The property offers CSX rail access, laydown yard, and proximity to NIWC and Charleston International Airport.
stories.impact: Charleston's industrial market is tightening and attracting institutional capital, signaling strong logistics and distribution demand driven by aerospace/defense (Boeing NIWC) and port activity. This supply absorption pressure and investor appetite indicate underlying job and population growth in Charleston metro; multifamily developers should anticipate near-term demand acceleration in Charleston residential submarkets, especially near Hanahan/North Charleston employment clusters—window to acquire sites ahead of supply tightness.

stories.title: NYC Pied-à-Terre Tax Rollout Temporarily Blocked
stories.excerpt: A real estate industry that has sounded alarms over New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s pied-a-terre tax harming the luxury residential market got a momentary reprieve Monday. Staten Island Supreme Court Justice Wayne Ozzi blocked the Mamdani administration’s rollout of a controversial surcharge on second homes worth more than $5 million and ordered the removal of nearly 1 million properties the city had posted online affected by the tax. The decision, which was issued in response to a lawsuit filed by homeowners last week, was appealed by the city Monday evening, which automatically triggered a stay of the ruling until an appeal is heard on Aug. 31. A source familiar with New York tax laws cautioned that no matter how the legal drama plays out, the tax is likely to still take effect even if delayed. The source said homeowners who received original July surcharge notices should “still get their paperwork ready.” The pied-a-terre tax was approved by the New York State Legislature in May and is projected to raise $500 million in revenue for the Big Apple, according to an analysis by New York City Comptroller Mark Levine. The policy has sparked concerns, however, from many real estate professionals about potential negative effects of luxury developers and buyers avoiding New York City despite the luxury market seeing an uptick in June. “We disagree with today’s ruling, but we are confident in both the pied-à-terre surcharge and the city’s ability to implement it fairly and effectively,” Mamdani spokesperson Matt Rauschenbach told the Wall Street Journal. “This surcharge asks those who own second homes valued at $5 million or more to contribute their fair share to the city they benefit from.” Andrew Coen can be reached at acoen@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Staten Island court blocked NYC pied-à-terre tax rollout; city appealed
Tax targets homes >$5M; $500M annual revenue projected
Uncertainty delays implementation; legal battle on Aug. 31; tax likely survives
stories.summary: Staten Island Supreme Court Justice Wayne Ozzi temporarily blocked New York City's pied-à-terre tax surcharge on second homes worth more than $5 million and ordered removal of ~1 million properties from the city's online list. The city appealed Monday, triggering a stay pending an Aug. 31 appeal hearing. Tax experts say the tax is likely to ultimately take effect despite legal challenges, though implementation may be delayed.
stories.impact: While directly a luxury condo issue, a sustained pied-à-terre tax reduces second-home investment demand in NYC and weakens developer appetite for luxury units in Manhattan/Brooklyn. However, it may shift capital toward primary-residence rental and workforce housing in NYC and suburban metros (NJ, CT, PA), opening rental demand and pricing windows for Class B/C multifamily developers outside prestige corridors. Monitor regulatory risk for similar taxes in other blue-state metros (CA, IL).

stories.title: The Hidden 90% of AI Costs Every CRE Firm Ignores
stories.excerpt: CRE firms have now moved through three technology cycles that each asked the same question at the wrong altitude: business intelligence in the 2000s, RPA in the 2010s, and generative AI now. Each time, the industry asks what the license costs. Two decades of watching these cycles play out says the license was never the number that mattered. The number that matters is what happens to cost per additional use case at the fifth deployment, the 20th, the 100th. Most CRE firms still can’t answer that question, and it’s costing them more than the license line ever will. The wrong approach is easy to spot. Most firms evaluate AI economics the way they’d evaluate traditional enterprise software: seat cost, contract length, implementation fee. That framing breaks once AI is deployed across a portfolio, because the real cost structure isn’t the license. It’s everything wrapped around it: integration, governance, maintenance, and the recurring labor of keeping a fast-moving technology from going stale. License cost is the visible 10 percent. The other 90 percent is where the budget actually goes, and almost nobody prices for it up front. It’s not that traditional CRE platforms are the wrong investment; they remain the operational backbone for many firms. The challenge is that AI introduces new economics that extend beyond the software purchase itself. Three cost models have played out at scale across this industry. All three break the same way, just on different timelines. The first is buying point solutions — a lease abstraction tool here, a market intelligence tool there, a separate product for tour books. Each tool stands on its own. But at scale, none of them share infrastructure. Each requires its own integration, governance and maintenance. The result is what the industry calls AI islands: real capability, zero compounding. This is a large part of why roughly 95 percent of generative AI pilots fail to produce measurable business impact. No market signal; advisory/operational issue only
stories.summary: An industry analysis warns CRE firms that the majority cost of AI deployment—integration, governance, maintenance, and labor—is typically not priced up front; the visible license cost represents only ~10% of total cost of ownership. stories.title: Owner Fisher Brothers Launches AI Innovation Lab
stories.excerpt: Real estate owner and operator Fisher Brothers announced Tuesday that it has launched an in-house artificial intelligence-native innovation lab. The 111-year-old Manhattan-based company’s AI Innovation Lab will operate across its commercial and residential enterprise, as well as at Area15, its Las Vegas entertainment venue. Rather than adopting off-the-shelf tools, Fisher Brothers’ technology team is developing proprietary applications and AI agents capable of automating multistep workflows, connecting previously siloed systems, and turning the company’s data into a resource employees can access and act on in real time, according to the firm. In doing so, Fisher Brothers joins other larger operators and owners in taking the proptech in-house more. “I feel like when ChatGPT went public to the consumer, that it was a watershed moment,” said Winston Fisher, a partner at Fisher Brothers, referring to the AI vehicle’s 2022 debut. “I quickly said that I think this is one of the most transformative technologies in the world. Our AI Innovation Lab is a culmination of working, becoming educated, and doing individual initiatives. Mark Stutzman, as our global chief technology officer, has been working on projects with our team over the last three years. That led us to the point where we could really take the next step: have a full-time dedicated resource over and above the existing team to really accelerate the transformation that we had already started working on.” In deploying a dedicated internal engineering team to develop company-owned AI applications, the lab will develop custom apps, foster agentic automation of repetitive workflows, connect internal systems, and expand AI fluency across the organization. bullets: Fisher Brothers launches proprietary AI Innovation Lab; applies to commercial + residential
In-house development of AI agents to automate workflows, integrate silos
Institutional operator investing in tech differentiation; no market demand signal
stories.summary: Fisher Brothers, a 111-year-old Manhattan owner/operator, announced launch of an in-house AI Innovation Lab serving its commercial, residential, and Area15 Las Vegas entertainment properties. The firm is developing proprietary AI agents to automate multistep workflows, integrate siloed systems, and enable real-time data access for employees. This represents institutional owners moving proptech development in-house.
stories.impact: No direct impact on multifamily supply, demand, capital availability, or cost. This is an operator efficiency play. Relevant only as a signal that larger institutional operators are building tech moats; smaller or regional multifamily developers may face operational cost disadvantages if proprietary AI/analytics become table-stakes for asset management and leasing.

stories.title: High Street Residential Tops Out on First Manhattan Development
stories.excerpt: High Street Residential (HSR), the residential subsidiary of Trammell Crow Company, has topped out construction on the firm’s first Manhattan project, The Marq, a 25-story luxury residential tower in SoHo. Slated for completion in the fourth quarter of 2027, the project will include 99 units, 2,072 square feet of ground-floor retail and 25 affordable apartments. Located on a vacant lot at 126 Lafayette St. in New York City’s Lower West Side, units at The Marq will range from studios to three-bedroom penthouses. “Our aim is for The Marq to reflect the vibrancy and elegance of this iconic community of SoHo,” said Michael Adamo, a principal with HSR in New York. “With its proximity to major transit hubs and green spaces like Hudson River Park, SoHo remains one of New York City’s most desirable locations for residential development. We’re proud to bring this project to life.” Along with its capital partners, other project partners on The Marq include Marvel Architects, general contractor Leeding Builders Group and interior designer Chris Shao Studio. bullets: High Street Residential (Trammell Crow subsidiary) tops out The Marq, Manhattan
25-story SoHo tower; 99 units + 25 affordable; completion Q4 2027
SUPPLY SIGNAL: Pipeline delivery in prime Manhattan submarket; mixed-income model
stories.summary: High Street Residential (HSR, Trammell Crow Company's residential subsidiary) topped out The Marq, a 25-story luxury residential tower at 126 Lafayette St. in SoHo, Manhattan. The project includes 99 market-rate units (studios to 3-bed penthouses), 2,072 SF of ground-floor retail, and 25 affordable apartments. Completion is scheduled for Q4 2027.
stories.impact: HSR's successful Manhattan entry and completion of premium SoHo unit validates luxury-infill development model in Lower Manhattan and signals Trammell Crow's confidence in NYC residential fundamentals despite office sector volatility. The 99-unit + 25-affordable mix reflects NYC's inclusionary zoning requirement, raising per-unit development cost; monitor whether this project's underwriting holds through 2027 delivery. SoHo/Lower West Side submarket will see supply absorption; developers should assess rent trajectory pre-delivery and weigh competing projects in immediate radius.

stories.title: Vietnamese Beauty Brand Hasaki Makes U.S. Debut in Cudahy
stories.excerpt: CBRE has arranged a 7,000‑square‑foot retail lease for Vietnamese beauty retailer Hasaki at Cudahy Plaza in Cudahy, marking the brand’s first U.S. store. Hai T. Dang with CBRE’s San Jose office represented the tenant. The landlord is Excel Realty Partners, LP. Cudahy Plaza, located at 7903–8017 South Atlantic Ave., is an open‑air retail center anchored by national retailers including Sprouts Farmers Market and Burlington. Founded in 2016, Hasaki is an omnichannel beauty and personal care retailer operating more than 300 stores, 18 clinics, and a nationwide e‑commerce platform in Vietnam. In addition to the Cudahy lease, CBRE represented Hasaki in a second 7,000-square-foot retail location at Magnolia Square, located at 1234 S. Magnolia Ave. in Anaheim, scheduled to open in the fourth quarter. “The center’s visibility, accessibility and heavy foot traffic aligned with Hasaki’s criteria for selecting a high‑performing location within Los Angeles County,” said Dang. Hasaki plans to open 10 additional U.S. stores The post Vietnamese Beauty Brand Hasaki Makes U.S. Debut in Cudahy appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Hasaki (Vietnam beauty retailer, 300+ stores) opens 2 US locations in SoCal
7K SF lease each in Cudahy + Anaheim; 10 additional US stores planned
Foreign brand expansion to US; reflects demographic/consumer shift in LA County
stories.summary: Vietnamese beauty brand Hasaki (founded 2016, 300+ stores in Vietnam) made its U.S. debut with a 7,000 SF lease at Cudahy Plaza (Cudahy, CA) and signed second 7K SF lease at Magnolia Square (Anaheim, CA), opening Q4 2024. The firm plans to open 10 additional U.S. stores. CBRE brokered both deals; landlords are Excel Realty Partners and other operators.
stories.impact: Signals Asian consumer brand migration to U.S., particularly SoCal, driven by Vietnamese and pan-Asian population concentration in LA County. While retail-focused, this underscores demographic and income growth in LA County suburbs (Cudahy, Anaheim, Orange County); multifamily developers should target workforce housing and Class B/C apartments near Vietnamese/Asian employment and retail clusters in LA County, anticipating sustained in-migration and household formation.

stories.title: PE Firm OceanSound Expands Presence at SL Green’s 450 Park Ave.
stories.excerpt: SL Green Realty Corp said Monday that OceanSound, LP has signed a new five-year, 32,032 square foot lease covering floors 8, 22 and 23 at 450 Park Ave. The private equity firm, which focuses on the technology sector, currently subleases 21,640 square feet “We’re proud to extend and expand our valued relationship with OceanSound at 450 Park Ave.,” said Steven Durels, EVP, director of leasing and real property at SL Green. “The recent completion of various building upgrades has positioned 450 Park as the premier boutique office building for tenants seeking best-in-class workspace with upscale amenities at a luxury location.” OceanSound was represented by John Johnson of Savills, Inc. SL Green was represented by Paul Amrich, Neil King, Alex D’Amario, Matthew Dichter and Brooke Dewing of CBRE. Located at the southwest corner of Park Avenue and 57th Street, 450 Park is a 33-story office tower whose tenants include Banco Bradesco, Blue Crest Capital Management, Garnett Station Partners, Muzinich & Co, and Steadfast Financial. The post PE Firm OceanSound Expands Presence at SL Green’s 450 Park Ave. appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: OceanSound (tech-focused PE firm) expands at SL Green's 450 Park Ave, Manhattan
32K SF new 5-year lease (floors 8, 22, 23); currently subleases 21.6K SF

stories.summary: OceanSound, LP, a private equity firm focused on technology, signed a new five-year, 32,032 SF lease at 450 Park Avenue in Midtown Manhattan, covering floors 8, 22, and 23. OceanSound currently subleases 21,640 SF at the property. SL Green completed building upgrades positioning 450 Park as a boutique, amenity-rich office option.
stories.impact: Reaffirms Manhattan Midtown office demand from high-value tenants (PE, tech) despite broader office sector headwinds. However, this is expansion within existing tenancy and sublease conversion—not new office-sector demand creation. Multifamily impact is indirect: continued Park Avenue/Midtown tenant retention supports worker base and nearby residential rental demand, but no new population influx; developers should focus on existing Midtown submarkets rather than anticipating new office-driven migration.

stories.title: MMCC Arranges Financing for Riverside County Self-Storage Property
stories.excerpt: Marcus & Millichap Capital Corporation (MMCC) arranged $7,380,000 in financing for Beaumont RV and Self Storage, a 49,958-square-foot self-storage property located at 251 W. 1st St. in Beaumont. Chad O’Connor, executive managing director in MMCC’s San Diego office, secured the 10-year financing with a national federal credit union on behalf of a private client. The loan carries a 5.75% interest rate and a 30-year amortization period. “Demand for self-storage remains supported by the sector’s durable operating fundamentals and the need for flexible space serving both household and recreational uses,” said O’Connor. “We were pleased to secure long-term financing with competitive terms that align with our client’s investment objectives.” Beaumont RV and Self Storage offers traditional self-storage units as well as dedicated RV and boat storage. The property is located near Interstate 10 and provides convenient access for customers throughout Beaumont and the surrounding Riverside County area. The post MMCC Arranges Financing for Riverside County Self-Storage Property appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: MMCC arranged $7.38M financing for Beaumont RV/Self-Storage, Riverside County
10-year loan at 5.75%; 30-year amortization; federal credit union lender
Self-storage fundamentals strong; capital available; no multifamily relevance
stories.summary: Marcus & Millichap Capital Corporation (MMCC) arranged $7.38 million in 10-year financing (5.75% rate, 30-year amortization) for Beaumont RV and Self Storage, a 49,958 SF property in Beaumont, Riverside County, California. The loan was secured from a national federal credit union. The property offers traditional self-storage, RV, and boat storage near I-10.
stories.impact: Not material to multifamily development. Self-storage is an alternative use class; while capital availability at 5.75% suggests credit union lending remains competitive for niche asset classes, this does not signal multifamily-specific debt markets, rate trends, or Riverside County residential demand. Self-storage demand may compete for same development sites in Riverside, but no direct supply/demand/capital signal for apartments.
